entities.name: Bankia
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Bankia, the Spanish financial institution created in 2011 through the forced merger of seven failing Spanish savings banks (cajas) including Caja Madrid (founded 1702) and Bancaja, became the central figure in Spain's 2012 banking crisis — when its €23.5 billion bailout request (the single largest in Spanish banking history) triggered the European Union's €100 billion Spanish bank bailout package and became the defining case of the European sovereign debt crisis's impact on Spain's financial system.

Bankia's creation was itself a product of Spain's property bubble collapse: the cajas (savings banks, traditional non-profit regional banks with political boards) had massively over-lent to Spain's property sector during the 2000s construction boom. When the 2008 financial crisis burst Spain's property bubble — the world's largest property bubble relative to GDP at its peak — the cajas' non-performing real estate loans destroyed their capital bases. The Spanish government forced their merger into Bankia, believing concentration would resolve their problems.

Bankia was briefly floated on the stock exchange in 2011, and investors (including many small Spanish retail savers who had been advised by Bankia's own branch staff to convert savings into shares) bought into the IPO — which was subsequently found to have contained materially false financial information. Bankia's 2012 bailout request wiped out shareholders and convertible bondholders, triggering thousands of legal actions. The Bankia scandal became Spain's most significant corporate governance and financial fraud case, with multiple executives including former Bankia CEO Rodrigo Rato (former IMF Managing Director) convicted of financial crimes. Bankia was eventually merged into CaixaBank in 2021.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bankia — whose collapse triggered Spain's €100 billion EU banking bailout, whose fraudulent IPO destroyed thousands of small investors' savings, and whose former CEO (a former IMF chief) was convicted of financial crimes — is the defining institution of Spain's devastating post-property-bubble banking crisis.
